clinicalPearls: Defined by autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis or Graves disease) occurring with at least one other organ-specific autoimmunity, but critically in the ABSENCE of adrenal insufficiency, hypoparathyroidism and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
Autoimmune thyroid disease is the obligatory anchor component around which the other autoimmune conditions cluster.

Conventionally subdivided: 3A thyroid plus another endocrine autoimmunity (e.g. type 1 diabetes), 3B thyroid plus gastrointestinal disease (pernicious anaemia, atrophic gastritis, coeliac disease), 3C thyroid plus skin/neuromuscular disease (vitiligo, alopecia, myasthenia gravis) and 3D thyroid plus connective tissue or haematological autoimmunity.
It is the most common of the adult autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes, with a strong female predominance and typical onset in middle adulthood.
Inheritance is polygenic with HLA class II associations (DR3/DR4), distinct from the monogenic AIRE defect of type 1 disease.
Autoantibodies (thyroid peroxidase, thyroglobulin, glutamic acid decarboxylase, parietal cell/intrinsic factor, tissue transglutaminase) may appear years before overt disease and guide surveillance.
Diagnosis of one autoimmune component should prompt periodic screening for others because components frequently emerge sequentially over years.
Adrenal involvement must be actively sought and excluded, as its presence reclassifies the syndrome as type 2 and signals life-threatening risk.
reference.pathophysiology: A polygenic loss of immune self-tolerance drives T-cell mediated and antibody-mediated destruction of multiple endocrine and non-endocrine tissues. Susceptibility is conferred principally by HLA class II haplotypes (DR3/DQ2 and DR4/DQ8) together with non-HLA immunoregulatory genes such as CTLA4 and PTPN22, distinguishing it from the monogenic AIRE-related type 1 syndrome. Autoimmune thyroid disease acts as the immunological hub, and shared genetic and environmental susceptibility predisposes affected individuals to accumulate further tissue-specific autoimmunity affecting pancreatic islets, gastric parietal cells, melanocytes, the neuromuscular junction or the gut. The defining biological feature, in contrast to type 2 disease, is sparing of the adrenal cortex, so mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid function remain intact.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APECED) with hypoparathyroidism, candidiasis and adrenal failure
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (Schmidt syndrome) with adrenal insufficiency
Isolated autoimmune thyroid disease without other components
IPEX syndrome in early-onset or male presentations
Systemic disorders mimicking multi-organ endocrine dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function testing with thyroid peroxidase, thyroglobulin and TSH-receptor antibodies
Glucose/HbA1c with islet autoantibodies (glutamic acid decarboxylase, IA-2, ZnT8)
Full blood count with vitamin B12, parietal cell and intrinsic factor antibodies for pernicious anaemia
Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase and endomysial antibodies)
Morning cortisol and ACTH stimulation testing to exclude adrenal involvement
Calcium, vitamin D and parathyroid assessment
Targeted antibody panels for suspected components such as acetylcholine receptor antibodies
redFlags: Features of adrenal insufficiency (postural dizziness, hyperpigmentation, salt craving, hyponatraemia) signalling progression and impending crisis
New profound fatigue, weight loss or unexplained hypoglycaemia suggesting evolving multi-gland failure
Bulbar or generalised weakness suggesting myasthenic crisis
Severe anaemia or subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
reference.prognosis: With early detection and hormone replacement of each affected gland the outlook is generally good. Lifelong surveillance is required because additional autoimmune components may emerge over years to decades.
pitfalls: Labelling a patient as type 3 without excluding adrenal disease, as unrecognised adrenal failure is dangerous and would reclassify the syndrome as type 2.
Discontinuing surveillance after treating one component and thereby missing later-emerging autoimmunity.
Overlooking non-endocrine components such as coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia or vitiligo that define the subtypes.
Attributing all fatigue to hypothyroidism when another gland is failing.
Failing to consider the diagnosis in first-degree relatives despite recognised familial clustering.
references: Clinical immunology guidance on organ-specific autoimmunity
management: Treat the anchoring autoimmune thyroid disease with levothyroxine for Hashimoto hypothyroidism or antithyroid drugs and definitive therapy for Graves disease
Manage associated components: insulin for type 1 diabetes, vitamin B12 replacement for pernicious anaemia and a gluten-free diet for coeliac disease
Treat other component autoimmunity as it arises, such as myasthenia gravis, vitiligo or alopecia
Confirm sparing of the adrenal cortex, distinguishing this syndrome from type 2 disease
Lifelong surveillance using organ-specific autoantibodies, which may precede overt disease, with periodic biochemical screening
Family screening and counselling given the HLA-linked polygenic susceptibility
